item.title: Tennessee Volunteers look to prove playoff credentials against top-ranked Texas Longhorns football
item.description: Arch Manning and the top-ranked Texas Longhorns face their toughest test yet against No. 14 Tennessee Volunteers in a Week 4 college football clash.
item.content:encoded:
Week 4 of the NCAA season is here, and we are starting to see a lot more ranked match-ups on the schedule. The first few weeks are typically designed so that bad teams can be beat up by the good teams. The good teams schedule them to figure out where they need to improve so that by the time Week 4 comes along, they can be ready for a tough match-up. However, not everyone takes that approach, and an example of that is here in the Texas vs. Tennessee game.

Texas comes into this game as the #1 ranked team in the nation. The Longhorns earned the honor after taking down Ohio State in a home game two weeks ago. That was sandwiched between two games that were laughable contests for the Longhorns. In Week 1, they demolished Texas State, winning 59-7. Last week, in Week 3, they won 30-6, again with no real struggle. The Ohio State game was quite the challenge, with Ohio State dominating the first half before Texas climbed back to win in the second half.

There are plenty of weapons on this Texas team, but most of the attention is going to fall on their quarterback, Arch Manning. It isn’t just because of Manning’s last name. He was the top prospect in football coming out of high school, and now is discussed as the top pick in the draft. He’s been just okay in college and even this season. For the year, Manning has thrown for 661 yards on 59-of-96 passes with seven touchdowns and two interceptions. He will need to be more accurate if he wants to lead Texas to a win in a hostile environment this weekend.

ARCH MANNING THROWS 2 TD PASSES AS TOP-RANKED TEXAS HOLDS OFF UTSA WITH SEC SCHEDULE LOOMING

Tennessee is the 14th-ranked team in the country and currently sits at a 3-0 record. A win today will catapult the Volunteers up the rankings and give them a legitimate chance to make the College Football Playoffs. I’m not sure it would completely derail Texas’s chance, but it would make their path more difficult. This is the first real test for Tennessee this season, and I’m interested to see if they can actually make this competitive.

In the first three games of the season, Tennessee has outscored opponents a combined 143 to 42. Two of those three games have been at home, where it is easier to win. On the road, they struggled a bit to stop Georgia Tech, which does give me concern about this team. Beating Furman and Kennesaw State at home isn’t quite as impressive an accomplishment. I suppose you can just be happy they took care of business when they needed to do it.

DONALD TRUMP ADDS POLITICAL STAKES, ANTICIPATION AND POTENTIAL SIDELINE CHAOS TO TEXAS-TENNESSEE SHOWDOWN

In order for Tennessee to win the game, they need to try and run the ball and milk the clock. Despite them putting up points at will this season, I can’t imagine they want to get into a shootout with the Longhorns. That strategy does seem to play into what the Volunteers want to do, as they’ve run the ball 133 times compared to just 74 pass plays.

I think Texas will win, but I’m not convinced they cover the full -4. Instead, the under is the way to go for me in this one as I expect a slower-paced game with both teams running and avoiding mistakes when possible. Give me under 55.5.

item.title: KFC unveils radically different restaurant in major comeback push
item.description: KFC's new Open House restaurant in McKinney, Texas, blends art deco design, digital ordering and table service to test breakfast and late-night dining that could shape future locations across America.
item.content:encoded:
A new KFC restaurant in McKinney, Texas, is about much more than debuting a new design.

"This is the Kentucky Fried comeback made real in one restaurant," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie told Fox News Digital.

The restaurant, dubbed Open House, serves as a testing ground for how the 75-year-old fast-food chain that Colonel Harland Sanders founded might modernize without abandoning the things that made it famous.

WHY KFC'S FRIED CHICKEN TASTES DIFFERENT FROM THAT OF EVERY OTHER FAST-FOOD CHAIN

KFC's challenge isn't necessarily getting Americans to remember the brand. It's getting them to think about it when deciding what to eat today.

"There is a massive love for this American icon," Tan-Gillespie said. But in the U.S., she added, "we tend to be thought about in people's memories. We're not actually being considered in eating moments of today."

That tension between nostalgia and relevance helped shape Open House. In developing the restaurant, KFC started with a question.

"We sat back and said, you know, if the Colonel were building a restaurant from scratch today, what would this look like?" Tan-Gillespie said.

AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY

The answer incorporates Art Deco and mid-century modern influences alongside large glass windows, digital ordering and drive-thru technology. At the same time, the restaurant features lobby hosts, table service, booths and outdoor dining designed to encourage customers to gather.

"For me, the philosophy is that we should be digital where it's helpful, but human where it matters," Tan-Gillespie said.

The menu follows a similar philosophy: Hold onto KFC's most recognizable products while experimenting with how customers want to eat chicken now, Tan-Gillespie said.

Buckets and the chain's original recipe remain central, but Open House expands into tenders, wings, sandwiches, wraps and nuggets, along with new sauces, drinks, snacks, sweets and sides.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Breakfast is part of the experiment, too. Open House is scheduled to operate from 6 a.m. to midnight, giving KFC an opportunity to test breakfast and late-night occasions that traditionally haven't been a major part of its U.S. business.

"We will see if those shoulder day parts work commercially for us and work for the guests, work for our team members," Tan-Gillespie said. "If they don't, we'll cut them back. And if they do, then we can look to scale them nationally."

KFC also chose McKinney with scalability in mind. Tan-Gillespie described the Dallas-Fort Worth area as a fast-growing and competitive restaurant market, while McKinney provides a mix of existing KFC customers and consumers the chain hopes to attract. The suburban setting also gives KFC a test that could potentially translate to similar markets elsewhere.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

But even as KFC experiments with new formats, flavors, technology and dayparts, Tan-Gillespie said some pieces of the brand aren't up for reinvention.

"Buckets of original recipe fried chicken should not change," she said. "I think the things that should change is making sure that we expand into the ways that customers want to eat fried chicken today."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

And what would Sanders make of that balance between the KFC he created and the one the company is trying to build?

"I think he would feel really proud, actually," Tan-Gillespie said. "I think he would say, 'This feels like me. This feels like what I was trying to do.' But for today."

item.title: BROADCAST BIAS: Media bash Sydney Sweeney, but cover for leftist Macklemore
item.description: Sydney Sweeney's Novig sports betting ad drew more negative broadcast coverage than rapper Macklemore's antisemitic remarks, which was typical for how the media handle celebrities.
item.content:encoded:
The broadcast networks can easily demonstrate their leftist bias in the way they cover entertainers. Those who use their fame for "good" are praised, and those who are the opposite – who lean Republican – are "controversial." Nowhere was that more evident than how the press freaked out about actress Sydney Sweeney vs. how they covered for antisemitic rapper Macklemore.

Sweeney, who identified as a registered Republican, keeps ending up on the "wrong" side of the networks. Last year, she made a provocative ad for blue jeans, making a pun with the word "good genes." ABC News warned: "The play on words is being compared to Nazi propaganda with racial undertones," and then invoked professor Robin Landa proclaiming the pun was racist: "The American Eugenics Movement and its prime between 1900 and 1940 weaponized the idea of good genes just to justify white supremacism."

Right now, Sweeney is featured in mostly naked advertisements for a sports prediction market called Novig. On Sept. 14, "CBS Mornings" carried the feminist water, weirdly claiming the ad demeaned women’s sports. Adriana Diaz proclaimed, "Actor Sydney Sweeney`s appearance in a provocative ad campaign is drawing backlash, especially from female athletes." She reported the four-time Olympic gold medalist swimmer Ariarne Titmus called the ad "a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft."

STEAMY SYDNEY SWEENEY AD DRAWS BACKLASH FROM FEMALE ATHLETES

Clearly, Sweeney’s ad was directed at men who are likely to bet on men’s sports. It was a weird claim. They noted that Sweeney responded with an Instagram post displaying athletes appearing mostly naked in ESPN Magazine’s "Body Issue."

Diaz pushed back: "So she is making that comparison, but people are really upset about this …. She is not an athlete herself and she is objectifying women – I mean, many people believe."

SYDNEY SWEENEY’S PROVOCATIVE SPORTS AD 'REINFORCES THE IMAGE SHE HAS ALREADY BUILT' DESPITE BACKLASH: EXPERT

Sweeney drew more negative coverage on the broadcast networks than Lindsay Clancy, who admitted to strangling her own three children. After her trial ended in a mistrial, the broadcast network coverage was 65% positive.

Sweeney also drew more negative coverage than the White rapper Macklemore – a stage name for Ben Haggerty – who was disinvited from several of performer Ed Sheeran’s concerts over his fervent talk of Israel’s alleged "genocide" in Gaza. On Sept. 15, ABC’s "World News Tonight" led the broadcast with "serious trouble" for Sheeran.

CRAIG CARTON: 'CRAZY PEOPLE' HATE SYDNEY SWEENEY, SUPPORT LINDSAY CLANCY

Anchor David Muir intoned: "We begin tonight with the political backlash playing out. Multiple performers now dropping out of singer Ed Sheeran's U.S. concert tour. It comes after Macklemore was removed as the opening act over remarks he made in support of Palestinians."

ABC reporter Whit Johnson vaguely suggested Macklemore’s song "Hind’s Hall" was "a song he wrote about the pro-Palestinian protests on college campuses." In typical fashion, the song touts "f--- the police" and implies they’re racist: "Has always been about dollars and the color of your pigment / but White supremacy is finally on blast / Screaming ‘Free Palestine’ 'til they're home at last." The lyrics include bashing Israel for colonialism, apartheid and genocide and attacking the "Nakba" – the Islamist term for "displacing the Palestinians" in creating Israel in 1948.

MACKLEMORE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER GETTING KICKED OFF ED SHEERAN TOUR AFTER PRO-PALESTINE STANCE

Macklemore’s schtick is so upside-down that he’s hailing pro-Hamas protests and then calling the immigration police of ICE a "terrorist organization."

On the "PBS News Hour," they brought on New York Times music-industry reporter Ben Sisario, who brought a similar vagueness about the Macklemore smears: "He also has a protest song that he released a couple of years ago, again about the war, and in it he accuses Israel of genocide, and he shows his solidarity with student protesters in the U.S. and in New York. So, his position has been widely known."

MACKLEMORE'S LONG HISTORY OF CONTROVERSY FROM GRAMMY WINS TO 'FREE PALESTINE' CONCERT REMARKS

Sisario tried to argue stadiums were more willing to allow antisemitic rapper Kanye West, and concluded: "I also think it is specifically about the political issue of the war in Gaza, and whether criticism of Israel's stance and Israel's actions in that war is considered allowable." PBS routinely blasts Israel as a global pariah.

Poor Sheeran could have toured with many apolitical pop acts – like some recent winners of "The Voice" or "American Idol" – but he chose a White rapper who built his career on confessing his "White privilege" and trashing White people, a man Daily Wire co-founder Ben Shapiro calls "the Colin Kaepernick of music," all about being celebrated by the left as a "social justice" champion.

Sheeran lamented, "I’ve tried in my career to not be a political commentator of any kind because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division, about humanity, not politics."

In response to the controversy, Macklemore announced a "Free Palestine Tour," scheduled for Dublin, Paris and London in October. item.title: Illegal immigrants, 89 and 73, accused of armed drug trafficking decades after sneaking into US
item.description: Cesar Valdes and Magdaleno Medina face felony cocaine trafficking and stolen firearms charges after an undercover Miami police operation uncovered drugs.
item.content:encoded:
Two illegal immigrants from Cuba with criminal records are behind bars after police say they were selling drugs and had stolen guns.

After their arrests, Cesar Valdes, 89, and Magdaleno Medina, 73, were found to have been in the country illegally – for more than 45 years.

Their recent trouble began after the Miami Police Department sent an undercover officer to purchase $60 worth of cocaine from Medina on Aug. 19, according to court records.

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF FENTANYL DEALING LINKED TO VIRGINIA HIGH SCHOOL OVERDOSES

After Medina allegedly sold the officer the drug, police returned to the "trailer" on Sept. 9 with a narcotics search warrant. They found Valdes there, too.

In their search, officers said they found dozens of clear bags of cocaine and marijuana, ammunition, stolen firearms and more than $4,800.

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WITH LENGTHY RAP SHEET AFTER ALLEGED JEALOUSY-FUELED KILLING

The men entered the country without inspection near Key West, Florida, on different days in May 1980, an ICE spokesman told Fox News Digital.

Medina has four prior felony convictions in the United States for cocaine smuggling, drug possession and drug trafficking, an ICE spokesman said. An immigration judge issued him a final order of exclusion July 24, 1996.

EXCLUSIVE: 5-TIME ILLEGAL ENTRANT ADMITS ‘MISTAKE’ THAT FINALLY GOT HIM BUSTED BY ICE

Final orders of exclusion were decisions made by immigration judges and issued before April 1997. That’s when a new system of removal proceedings began, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The details of Medina’s prior arrests and convictions were unavailable. It was unclear whether he spent any time in jail.

ICE-LED FLORIDA OPERATION NETS 500 — INCLUDING ILLEGAL ALIENS ACCUSED OF MURDER, CHILD ABUSE, CARTEL TIES

Valdes has a record of previous charges in Miami-Dade County, including cocaine possession and probation violation in the 1980s and 1990s. It was unclear whether he spent any time in jail.

Valdes was issued a final order of exclusion by an immigration judge on March 10, 1993.

SEND US A TIP

Medina currently faces eight felony charges, including possession of cocaine with the intent to sell, cocaine trafficking and illegal possession of a firearm and ammunition as a convicted felon. Valdes is facing five similar drug- and firearm-related felony charges.

GOT A TIP?

Both men are being held in a Miami jail with ICE detainers.

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences," an ICE spokesman told Fox News Digital in an email.

"Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S. We will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you."

Medina and Cesar have pleaded not guilty to their charges in Miami-Dade County. The attorney representing both men declined to comment on their cases.

item.title: PRESIDENT PAZ: Bolivia has rejected socialism and is open for business
item.description: Bolivia's leader outlines a shift from socialism to "capitalism for everyone," seeking United States investment in lithium, copper, and natural gas.
item.content:encoded:
Bolivia is beginning a new chapter.

For nearly two decades, my country was governed by the Movement Toward Socialism. That period reshaped Bolivia’s economy, institutions, and relationship with the United States. Today, my government is taking a different direction: rebuilding confidence, strengthening institutions, opening the economy to investment, and creating more room for private enterprise and entrepreneurship.

When I took office, Bolivia’s Central Bank had only $51 million in reserves. Ten months later, reserves had risen to close to $1.2 billion, and our objective is to continue rebuilding them. Inflation remains high, fuel shortages have tested our people, and the work ahead is difficult. But the direction is clear: Bolivia is putting its economic house in order.

TRUMP ADMIN BACKS BOLIVIA STATE OF EMERGENCY AS LEFTIST EX-LEADER'S LOYALISTS FRACTURE NATION

During my campaign, I described our approach as "capitalism for everyone." By that I mean access to capital, the ability to invest, the freedom to build businesses, and the opportunity to create jobs and prosperity. Ideology does not put food on the table. Employment does. Production does. Investment does. Economic growth does.

This new economic direction is also creating the basis for a new relationship with the United States. My discussions in New York with Secretary of State Marco Rubio reflected an important change in the relationship between our countries. Bolivia seeks cooperation with the United States based on mutual respect, economic opportunity, security, investment, and shared interests.

THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

The Trump administration has placed renewed attention on the Western Hemisphere, including economic strength, security, and cooperation among the nations of the Americas. Bolivia intends to engage constructively in that conversation while pursuing its own national interests and rebuilding relationships that can contribute to growth and stability.

Bolivia is open for business. But opening our economy does not mean selling our future.

RESOURCE-RICH NATION PRAISES US TIES AMID WASHINGTON-BEIJING CRITICAL MINERALS RACE

Our country possesses extraordinary natural wealth. We have natural gas, agricultural capacity, forests, and strategic minerals including lithium, copper, and tin that are increasingly important to the global economy. But we do not want to repeat the history of countries that exported their natural resources for decades while remaining poor.

Bolivia cannot simply remove minerals from the ground, ship them abroad, and watch other countries create the technology, manufacturing, jobs, and value from them. We want long-term partnerships built around employment, training, technology, infrastructure, productivity, and value added in Bolivia.

AFRICAN GROWTH BOOM FOLLOWS TRUMP PUSH TO REPLACE AID WITH TRADE

Our message to American and international investors is straightforward: Bolivia welcomes investment, capital, technology, and expertise. We want companies that are prepared to build, produce, employ, train, and grow alongside Bolivian workers and businesses.

As I told the United Nations, Bolivia wants to be open to the world with dignity.

US, SHIELD OF THE AMERICAS CONDEMN 'ONGOING EFFORTS' TO OVERTHROW BOLIVIA'S ELECTED PRESIDENT AMID UNREST

That means economic growth must also serve the Bolivian people. A stronger private sector does not mean abandoning social responsibility. Our objective is to create better jobs, stronger institutions, better education, greater security, and more opportunity. We must protect our forests and the Amazon, respect our Indigenous communities, and ensure that development creates tangible benefits for the people who live here.

The same principle applies to our young people. Bolivia’s future will depend on whether they can find purpose, work, and opportunity at home. Investment should help create that future.

TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

Bolivia’s economic direction is therefore based on a simple proposition: work with the United States, our neighbors, and the wider world; welcome productive investment; encourage entrepreneurship; expand private enterprise; and ensure that the wealth created in Bolivia also improves the lives of Bolivians.

Not everything has been resolved. We are only beginning.

But Bolivia will not remain on its knees. We will stand up, move forward, and build again.

item.title: Legendary agent Leigh Steinberg explains why fans should not be concerned about this 0-2 team
item.description: Legendary agent Leigh Steinberg says Jim Harbaugh's track record means the 0-2 Los Angeles Chargers will make adjustments and contend for a playoff spot.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Chargers are one of eight teams to begin the season 0-2 and are desperate for a spark.

Since the expansion of the playoff format in 2020, just 16% of 0-2 teams have reached the postseason. Even though the Chargers lost to the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, two games in which they entered as heavy favorites, legendary agent Leigh Steinberg is not willing to write off the Chargers just yet.

Why? Because of head coach Jim Harbaugh.

LEGENDARY AGENT LEIGH STEINBERG HAS SIMPLE ADVICE FOR GIANTS STAR JAXSON DART AFTER CRUSHING KNEE INJURY

"At the end of the day, I think, Jim Harbaugh is one of the most effective and unique coaches in the history of pro football," Steinberg told OutKick in a recent interview.

"And the fact that they’ve lost two games, there are 15 left, and they’ll make adjustments, they can see what’s happening on the film, they understand that if you’re fumbling the ball multiple times and (committing) turnovers, but, I’d be very surprised if they weren’t in the playoff hunt."

The Chargers entered the season with hopes of contending in the AFC, with plenty of excitement surrounding Mike McDaniel as their offensive coordinator. In McDaniel’s first two games, the Chargers have a minus-4 turnover differential and have averaged just 14 points per game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Chargers have gone 11-6 in each of Harbaugh’s first two seasons at the helm, losing in the wild-card round each time. Right now, finishing 11-6 seems like a tall task for a Chargers team that has struggled, especially considering they have a difficult upcoming schedule.

In their next six games, the Chargers play the Buffalo Bills, Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos, Kansas City Chiefs, Los Angeles Rams and Houston Texans.

With the slow start and the grueling schedule, some are wondering if Harbaugh is already on the hot seat. Steinberg said any talk of Harbaugh, or any coach, being on the hot seat is premature.

"There’s not a ton of storylines at this point in the season, so people have a tendency to overreact to 2 weeks. It's only been two weeks, it's just too early to consign someone," Steinberg said.

While it’s still early in the season, if the offense doesn’t turn things around over the next six games and the Chargers find themselves a few games under .500 at the midpoint of the season, falling behind in a strong AFC West, it could get late early for Harbaugh and Los Angeles.

Steinberg, who was inducted into the California Sports Hall of Fame in 2017, has had many high-profile clients throughout his impressive career. Across football and baseball, Steinberg’s clients include Steve Bartkowski, Steve Young, Troy Aikman, Warren Moon, Bruce Smith, Thurman Thomas, Kordell Stewart, Jeff George, Ben Roethlisberger, Myron Rolle, Matt Leinart, Mark Brunell, Ricky Williams, Howie Long, Eric Karros and Dusty Baker, among others.

item.title: NFL legend Brian Urlacher rips Colin Kaepernick, says protests wouldn't have flown in his locker room
item.description: Brian Urlacher says Colin Kaepernick's NFL anthem kneeling would have been a "line in the sand" if they shared a Chicago Bears locker room together.
item.content:encoded:
Colin Kaepernick's infamous protests during the 2016 NFL season are still talked about to this day, but Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher made it clear something like that wouldn't have flown if he was in the same locker room.

The legendary Chicago Bears linebacker talked about Kaepernick's knee-taking and locker room dynamics in general during an appearance on OutKick's "The Craig Carton Show."

Carton asked Urlacher if politics were a big thing in the Bears' locker room while he was playing in the league.

PATRIOTS LEGEND ROB GRONKOWSKI REVEALS THE IMPACT POLITICS HAS ON LOCKER ROOM DYNAMICS

"No," Urlacher said. "Politics — I didn't even know what I was (politically) back then. I didn't care, man... You can't have the racial divide in the locker room. It's just not going to work. If you do, your team is going to be s---."

Urlacher pointed out that everyone in the room is coming together to work toward the same goal, but Kaepernick's anthem protests? That wouldn't have flown with him.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"The thing with him taking a knee would have been really, really f---king hard for me to put up with in the locker room," he said. "That would have been something that would have probably been a line in the sand for me when it comes to stuff like that."

He and Carton both agreed that in the locker room, all that matters is that you're there, not how you got there; an idea that Carton said should probably be applied to society at large.

Urlacher agreed.

"We have to get along (in the locker room)," he said. "There are going to be spats, don't get me wrong. There are some times where you get into it with your teammates, but then literally 30 minutes later it's squashed. You're over it. You're moving on."

But again, that whole thing with Kaepernick was different. In fact, it turned him off from the league for years.

"I'd retired, so I was watching all this happen on TV, and we quit watching. There were probably two, two and a half, three years where we didn't watch football. I was like, as long as this s---'s taking place, I'm not watching. My wife was fully on board. She's all about that as well. So we just didn't watch pro football for a few years there because of all the s--- that was going on."

item.title: Put down those textbooks and turn off the screens. Here is a great way for kids to learn
item.description: Charlotte Mason's "living books" philosophy offers a powerful alternative to bland textbooks, transforming how children learn through great literature.
item.content:encoded:
It’s late September. Kids are firmly back in school; routines are established and reading lists set. But what exactly is on the menu? The usual textbooks, which, if they’re in a government school, are often written by committee (with an agenda), range from uninspiring to outright woke.

Or maybe most of your child’s school curriculum is delivered via lifeless and impersonal computer screens.

But there is an alternative, a source whose advocacy first transformed the task of educating children over one hundred years ago. Virtually unknown to public school parents, the British 19th-century reformer Charlotte Mason (1842-1923) has long been the hero of modern homeschooling in America, and the movement’s best-kept secret weapon.

WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO

But her ideas and theories are not just applicable to the home-schooling community. Parents and educators can greatly benefit from Mason’s ideas about children and reading, which are even more relevant today.

Creating a thirst for knowledge, and lifelong love of learning was Mason’s goal. If children developed an early hunger for ideas, she reasoned, it would sustain them through their lives. Mason believed that in addition to the proper vitamins and nutrients needed to thrive, children require ideas to chew on, to properly grow. And the source of these ideas, she reasoned, was not typical textbooks.

BEN CARSON, RILEY GAINES FIGHT SCRUBBING OF FAITH FROM KIDS' US HISTORY BOOKS FOR AMERICA'S 250TH

That’s a perspective as true today as it was in Mason’s time. Most if not all textbooks which children encounter in public schools are either bland by design, so as not to arouse controversy, or the opposite: brazenly geared to advance a woke agenda.

Mason believed that the best resource for the ideas that will benefit children most came from a regular exposure to great art, great music, and, above all, books of "literary quality" or great books. "For the best thought the world possesses is stored in books," she wrote in "Parents and Children." "Children must have books, living books ... the best is not too good for them; anything less than the best is not good enough."

DOLLY PARTON'S BELOVED LITERACY MISSION SEES SURGE OF SUPPORT AFTER COUNTRY ICON'S DEATH

Her idea of "living books" was about books written by a single author (not a committee), ones that actively engage the mind, imagination and spirit, rather than simply presenting factual material.

For example, a list of "living books" for early learners (grades 1-4) might include: "The Trumpet of the Swan," "Black Beauty," and "A Little Princess." Titles for middle schoolers include: "My Side of the Mountain," "Around the World in 80 Days," "To Kill a Mockingbird," and C.S. Lewis’s classic "Narnia" series.

CLASSICAL EDUCATION AND AI COULD RESHAPE HOW AMERICA PREPARES ITS CHILDREN

High school students can gain most from reading "Pride and Prejudice," "David Copperfield," and, "Through Gates of Splendor," as well as the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy.

Living books like these can spark kids’ curiosity, thanks to their authors’ genuine passion for their subject.

WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI CAN MIMIC A TEACHER, BUT IT CANNOT SHEPHERD A SOUL

Unlike textbooks, they use a compelling, even spellbinding style that draws the student into the plot and characters, triggering their imagination and emotions.

Living books like "My Side of the Mountain" and "To Kill a Mockingbird" weave sometimes complex concepts and subjects into an approachable narrative, in ways that allow children to more easily connect and identify with the material. Like those of us who grew up with favorite books, children are bound to remember details and themes, long after the work has been returned to the shelf.

GEORGIA SCHOOL DISTRICT DEFENDS PULLING 'SEXUALLY EXPLICIT' BOOK DEPICTING CHILD RAPE AMID 'CENSORSHIP' CLAIMS

Living books often feature unfamiliar words and language that challenge young readers to expand their vocabulary. Contrary to what lazy teachers may think, old-fashioned forms of communicating in English, like Charles Dickens’s novels or even the King James Bible, don’t turn off young minds. They broaden and deepen a reader’s grasp of the English language, which is crucial for their intellectual, even moral, growth.

For instance, E. B. White, author of classics like "Charlotte’s Web," and "The Trumpet of the Swan," never hesitated to challenge his young readers with new words like "radiant" and "humble," because he believed, like Charlotte Mason, that children were smart, capable readers.

AMERICAN SCHOOLS COST MORE THAN EVER BUT OUR STUDENTS STILL KEEP FAILING

White once said, "Anyone who writes down to children is simply wasting his time. You have to write up, not down. Children are demanding. They are the most attentive, curious, eager, observant, sensitive, quick, and generally congenial readers on earth.... Children are game for anything. I throw them hard words and they backhand them across the net."

Finally, unlike typical textbooks, living books help students move from a passive learning mode to an active learning mode. Instead of simply memorizing what they need to know to pass a test, having students retell a story like "The Little Princess" in their own words, builds lasting communication and analytical skills.

Try some living books out on your children if you haven’t already. Books like Louisa May Alcott’s "Little Women" will teach them lessons about the importance of family, sacrifice, and generosity. item.title: Wave of overlooked 'left-wing' lawsuits could come with an unexpected price tag for Americans
item.description: A report from Power The Future and the Heritage Foundation warns climate lawsuits could cost American households nearly $1,465 more per year.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: American households could end up paying $1,465 more per year on average in energy costs if "anti-energy" climate lawsuits against oil and gas companies are successful, according to a new report first obtained by Fox News Digital.

Americans will "pay a lot more" if the far-left "get their way," warned Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J Antoni, who co-authored the report with Power The Future founder Daniel Turner.

Hundreds of lawsuits and other state-level "climate superfund" laws could increase the cost of gasoline, electricity and other everyday necessities Americans rely on, the report estimates.

SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA

The new analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear a closely-watched lawsuit next month out of Boulder, Colorado, which could drastically shape the future of climate litigation.

"If those folks on the radical left wing who are anti-energy, if they get their way, your costs are going to go up," Antoni told Fox News Digital. "Your household is going to pay a lot more. The energy is going to get much more expensive."

"You may think it's bad now, but it will get significantly worse," he added.

The report estimates energy companies could face an additional $194 billion in annual costs, which the authors argue would ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices rather than absorbed entirely by companies or their shareholders.

Those costs could add roughly 41 cents to a gallon of gasoline and increase residential electricity rates by about 8.6%, according to the analysis.

"Every single time a company is sued, yes, they pay some damages, but ultimately they will just charge people more for their product to recoup those losses," Turner told Fox News Digital.

LAWSUITS COST EVERY AMERICAN HOUSEHOLD THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS. SUPREME COURT CAN HELP

The report examined more than 300 pending lawsuits, three state "climate superfund" laws, 12 state legislative proposals and one federal bill. Its estimate reflects a "full-success scenario" in which all of those measures prevail; it does not predict that they will.

The analysis counted each lawsuit only once and excluded duplicate filings. In fact, Antoni said the estimate may be conservative because some lawsuits do not specify the damages they are seeking, leaving potential court awards open-ended.

The legal efforts include New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act, which was blocked by a federal judge in August, and the Supreme Court’s pending Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County case.

That case could determine whether state and local governments can pursue climate lawsuits against fossil fuel companies in state court.

GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'HIDDEN CLIMATE TAX' HITTING AMERICANS NATIONWIDE, LAWMAKER WARNS

Turner argued the lawsuits could also shift responsibility away from state and local leaders.

"The concern about these superfund lawsuits is that they absolve elected leaders from doing the bad, boring part of governing, which is infrastructure and mitigation strategies," he said.

Despite the rise in climate lawsuits and state "superfund" laws, Antoni said the issue has largely flown under the radar.

"It really is important that we start ringing the alarm bells now before these things actually come to pass and American families have to foot the bill for it," he said.

item.title: Mistress may have handed prosecutors missing ‘why’ in ‘American Idol’ alum’s wife murder case: expert
item.description: The Caleb Flynn trial took a dramatic turn as mistress Alleigha Botner read explosive texts exchanged in the months before Ashley Flynn's fatal shooting.
item.content:encoded:
The explosive testimony of Caleb Flynn's former mistress may have handed Ohio prosecutors a critical piece of their murder case against the former "American Idol" contestant – a potential answer to why he would allegedly kill his wife, a former prosecutor told Fox News Digital.

"Motive. She provides a motive," Josh Ritter, a former prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor, said of Alleigha Botner's testimony. "She gives jurors a reason for why would this man murder his wife."

"She seems like she was, by all accounts, a very nice woman," Ritter said about Ashley Flynn. "She's the mother of his children. Yes, he wanted out of the marriage."

"Perhaps there was some financial gain in the idea of life insurance, but, you know, jurors oftentimes struggle with that question," he added.

DAD OF 'AMERICAN IDOL' CONTESTANT'S SLAIN WIFE MADE EERIE GOOGLE SEARCH AFTER HEARING OF HER MURDER

Flynn is accused of fatally shooting his wife in the back of the head inside their Ohio home on Feb. 16 and staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges.

Botner, who testified she carried on an affair with Flynn for roughly a year and a half, spent two days walking jurors through many of the 107,000-plus messages exchanged during their relationship.

NEW JERSEY MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING WIFE WITH BARBELL ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED IN MESSAGES TO RELATIVES: REPORT

Some contained explicit discussions about Ashley's death.

In one May 2025 message, Flynn allegedly wrote, "If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat."

RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES

Days later, he allegedly wrote, "I hate her, loathe her. I want her dead."

In June, Flynn allegedly told Botner, "Please hire someone to take [her] out. I need you in my life, I need you."

SCOTT PETERSON'S DEFENSE LOSES BID TO INTRODUCE WITNESS TESTIMONY IN LONG-RUNNING FIGHT TO OVERTURN CONVICTION

Botner responded, "So tempting. I can't live without you. And I've had this thought so often lately. How do we figure this out?"

Botner also became emotional while reading one of her own messages to Flynn, expressing regrets that she wished she never wrote it.

ALEX MURDAUGH LAWYERS ALLEGE ‘FABRICATED’ EVIDENCE WAS USED TO SECURE MURDER INDICTMENTS

"I want to kill her, Caleb," she had written.

"That makes two of us," Flynn allegedly responded.

ALEX MURDAUGH MAKES 'EXPLOSIVE' BID TO BLOW UP MURDER CASE HINGING ON DNA, DIRTY MONEY AND LIES: EXPERT

Ritter said it is the substance of those exchanges – rather than simply the existence of the affair or sheer volume of messages – that could prove significant for prosecutors.

"It's the idea that he's even discussing her being dead," Ritter said. "He went as far as to saying I literally would kill her. That's far beyond someone voicing their frustrations and venting to a lover that I wish my wife wasn't around, I wish she would leave, I wish we could get a divorce."

"This is saying you want that person dead, that, in your view, that is your solution to the problem that you have," he added.

The messages grew particularly significant as prosecutors moved jurors closer to the night Ashley was killed.

FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON FOUND GUILTY OF MURDERING ATTORNEY WHO VANISHED FROM BLOODY OFFICE

Botner testified that Flynn told her in an August message he had stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail."

Months later, Botner gave Flynn a Jan. 11 ultimatum to leave Ashley or she would end their relationship. When he failed to do so, Botner cut off communication until Feb. 14 – just two days before Ashley's death.

By the night of Feb. 15, the two were communicating again.

Botner testified that Flynn discussed his plans for the following day, including telling family members about the divorce and obtaining a burner phone.

Shortly after midnight, Flynn allegedly wrote to Botner, "It's happening."

He then wrote, "February 16th – day I'll never forget."

"You're about to be free," Botner responded.

"I choose you," Flynn replied.

Those were some of the final messages Flynn sent Botner before she learned Ashley had been killed, she testified.

Ritter pointed to that timing as among the most significant evidence Botner brought to the prosecution's case.

He noted that Flynn had spent months allegedly talking about wanting Ashley dead before the messages reached the eve of her killing.

"The day before the murder takes place, he tells his mistress that tomorrow is going to be a big day, that he chooses her," Ritter explained. "He's made a decision and that tomorrow, meaning February 16th, the date his wife was murdered, will be a day that he will never forget."

But Ritter said the same enormous volume of messages prosecutors are using against Flynn also gives his attorneys an argument.

The defense can contend prosecutors have cherry-picked the most damaging statements from more than 100,000 messages exchanged during an intense affair and stripped them of the broader context of two people using exaggerated and sometimes ugly language.

Flynn's attorneys can also argue that when he talked about what would happen Feb. 16, he was referring to finally leaving Ashley – not killing her.

WATCH: Caleb Flynn had ominous response when mistress said ‘I want to kill her’

"That could be true," Ritter said. "It could be that he is just the unluckiest man on earth, that the day he tells his mistress he's going to announce to his wife that he's leaving her after months of saying that he wants her dead, that some random home burglar happens to break in with no signs of forced entry, goes to his vehicle, knows exactly where to find his handgun, marches upstairs, puts two bullets in the back of his wife's head while she's sleeping, and leaves the rest of the house undisturbed."

During cross-examination Thursday, Flynn's attorneys began putting Botner's own language before the jury.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"I'm so done with you. You have murdered my heart," Botner acknowledged writing Flynn during one argument. "I hope you're glad you took my virginity and also my heart and stomped all over it. Enjoy your marriage. I'm done."

The defense also has another potentially important distinction to emphasize, Ritter said. Despite Flynn's repeated statements about wanting Ashley dead, he never explicitly told Botner he intended to carry out her killing.

"There was never an explicit mention of, 'I'm going to do it, I'm gonna follow through on it,'" Ritter said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I think they are also going to concentrate on the idea, as they have since opening statements, that this might have been a rush to judgment, that once police uncovered the affair, they stopped their investigation," Ritter said. "And once they knew that he was planning on leaving his wife, they thought, 'Well, that's enough for us. We're not going to pursue other leads.'"

"I'm not saying that's a convincing argument, but I'm saying that that is at least something for them to stand on and mount a defense on his behalf," he added.

WATCH: Caleb Flynn mistress drops bombshells in dramatic testimony

SEND US A TIP

The defense can also point to the absence of the alleged murder weapon, an eyewitness to the shooting and gunshot residue on Flynn.

GOT A TIP?

Botner testified, however, that Flynn had previously shown her a gun he kept inside the center console of his truck, though she could not remember what it looked like.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"In an ideal world, would the prosecution want the murder weapon? Sure," Ritter said. "But ... it's something that the defense is obviously going to lean into."

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

But for Ritter, Botner's testimony ultimately comes back to the question prosecutors hope jurors will ask when they consider the killing – why?

item.title: Delivery drones could be waiting before you even order
item.description: Flytrex says its AI-powered Rooftop Dock system in Dallas-Fort Worth positions drones at restaurants before orders arrive, cutting delivery costs by 60%.
item.content:encoded:
Your next food delivery could start moving before you even place the order. Flytrex is rolling out a system in Dallas-Fort Worth that sends drones to restaurant rooftops ahead of expected demand. AI predicts which locations are likely to get busy, then positions an aircraft nearby. If the prediction is right, the drone is already waiting when your food is ready. Flytrex says its new Rooftop Dock and predictive fleet positioning can cut its own delivery costs by 60%. The company also says customer delivery times can drop by half. The idea makes a lot of sense. Stop wasting time sending a drone to the restaurant after the food is ready. So how does Flytrex know where to put a drone before anyone orders, and how could this expand beyond Texas?

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Get Better Healthcare With AI replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay now at CyberGuyLive.com

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

Flytrex uses machine-learning models to study past demand, location and the time of day. The software also looks at other activity across its delivery network. It then predicts which restaurants are most likely to receive upcoming orders. Instead of leaving every available drone at a central location, Flytrex can send aircraft closer to restaurants before customers order anything. That could make a big difference during busy meal periods. A pizza restaurant that usually sees a rush around dinner time could already have a drone waiting nearby. Once an order comes through and the kitchen finishes the food, the aircraft can get moving quickly. The current process can take longer. An operator may have to send a drone from another location after the restaurant has the order. The aircraft then flies to the restaurant before it can start the customer delivery. Flytrex wants to cut out that extra trip.

Once Flytrex decides where a drone should wait, the aircraft lands on its Rooftop Dock. The company says the system can go on an existing rooftop or another elevated area near the restaurant. According to Flytrex, the setup does not require additional real estate or structural changes. The company also says it can operate without placing a Flytrex employee at each restaurant. After the drone lands, it shuts down its motors and waits. When the food is ready, the aircraft lowers a hook into position. A restaurant employee clips the packaged order onto it without handling the drone. Then the aircraft takes off and heads directly toward the customer. That also removes the need for someone to carry the food to a separate drone launch site. Flytrex co-founder and CEO Amit Regev says those last few hundred feet between the restaurant kitchen and the aircraft have been one of the harder parts of drone delivery. "The truly challenging part has never been the flight; it's the last few hundred feet between the kitchen and the aircraft," Regev said.

Sending a drone to a restaurant before an order arrives could save more than time. Flytrex says its new setup cuts its cost per delivery by 60%. The company also says it can reduce customer delivery times by half. The drone no longer has to make a separate pickup flight from a central location. Meanwhile, restaurant workers can load the order without a dedicated Flytrex employee standing there. That could let each aircraft handle more deliveries over the course of a day. There is one big variable, though. The AI needs to put the drone in the right place. Customer demand can change quickly. Weather can shift ordering patterns. A local event could suddenly make one restaurant much busier than expected. If a drone ends up waiting at the wrong location, Flytrex may have to move it again.

Flytrex is launching the technology at active merchant locations across Dallas-Fort Worth. The company says it is also installing the system at more than 100 additional sites. That makes North Texas an important test for something Flytrex wants to expand much further. The company says it has completed more than 250,000 U.S. deliveries. It has also been building relationships with some of the biggest names in food delivery. In 2025, Uber invested in Flytrex through a partnership focused on Uber Eats orders. We covered that move when Uber Eats began preparing for drone deliveries.

Flytrex also partnered with DoorDash in Dallas-Fort Worth. DoorDash has since expanded its own drone ambitions. We recently covered how DoorDash received FAA approval for its commercial drone delivery operation.

CLEVELAND CLINIC LAUNCHES PRESCRIPTION DRONE DELIVERY

Flytrex has another important piece in place as it looks beyond Texas. The company received Federal Aviation Administration approval for beyond visual line of sight operations, also known as BVLOS. That allows Flytrex to conduct approved flights without requiring a visual observer to keep each aircraft in direct sight throughout the trip. Instead, Flytrex can monitor multiple drones remotely from an operations center under the conditions of its authorization. Flytrex says the approval gives it a path toward expanding into the 37 largest U.S. metropolitan areas. That does not mean rooftop drone delivery will appear across all 37 markets at once. Flytrex still has to build out its network as it expands. The new rooftop system gives the company a setup it hopes to repeat from one market to the next.

The rooftop system comes after several other moves from Flytrex. In April 2026, the company introduced its Sky2 delivery drone through a partnership with Little Caesars. The aircraft can carry up to 8.8 pounds, enough to handle two large pizzas. Flytrex also opened a manufacturing facility in Pilot Point, Texas. The company says the site can produce about 1,000 drones per year. Now Flytrex is tackling the next problem. Building more drones only gets you so far if those aircraft spend too much time traveling to pickup locations. Putting them closer to the restaurants before orders arrive could keep more of that fleet moving toward customers.

If Flytrex gets this right, you could spend less time staring at a delivery timer. The drone may already be waiting at the restaurant when your food is ready, so it can head toward your home almost immediately. That could also mean your meal spends less time sitting around before pickup. Then there is the cost. Flytrex says the system cuts its own delivery costs by 60%. The company has not said whether those savings will eventually lead to lower fees for customers, but a cheaper delivery model could make drone delivery easier to expand. Don't expect a drone hovering over your takeout spot tomorrow. Flytrex is starting in Dallas-Fort Worth, and expanding this kind of service will take time. The bigger takeaway is what happens before the drone ever takes off. If AI can put the aircraft where the next order is likely to happen, Flytrex could make the whole process faster without asking customers to do anything differently.

CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS

What gets my attention here is how simple the problem sounds once Flytrex points it out. The drone may be fast in the air, but that does not help much if it has to spend part of the delivery flying to the restaurant first. Moving drones ahead of demand could change that. The AI looks for where orders are likely to come from, while the rooftop dock gives the aircraft somewhere to wait. If Flytrex can get those predictions right consistently, it could cut a lot of wasted time out of each delivery. Dallas-Fort Worth should give us a good sense of whether this works beyond a handful of restaurants. Flytrex says more than 100 additional installations are underway, which should give the company plenty of chances to prove whether those big claims about speed and cost hold up.

Would faster food delivery be worth having drones waiting on restaurant rooftops around your community, or would you rather keep all that buzzing out of your neighborhood? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: The frat omertà: Whistleblower warns of ‘code of silence’ after Ole Miss deaths, alleged Penn State coke ring
item.description: The Ole Miss student death and Penn State cocaine ring allegations echo a deeper crisis in Greek life, says fraternity hazing survivor Andrew Lohse.
item.content:encoded:
"You need a code of omertà if you're trying to create an organization that's essentially like a criminal organization," Andrew Lohse said.

Lohse was talking about fraternities – the 36-year-old is a fraternity hazing survivor and the author of "Confessions of an Ivy League Frat Boy."

As a Dartmouth student, the whistleblower exposed the stomach-turning indoctrination rituals he said he endured inside Sigma Alpha Epsilon.

TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS

When recent headlines came to light regarding the mysterious deaths of two students at Ole Miss – one of whom was in a fraternity – and the alleged frat cocaine distribution ring at Penn State, Lohse said he was immediately reminded of his time as a brother.

"For years and years [the last] 10 years, it's like whenever someone dies in a frat, like that's when my phone rings," Lohse told Fox News Digital.

OLE MISS NAMES STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS OFFICIAL ADDRESSES POTENTIAL FOR FOUL PLAY

One of the Ole Miss students who was found dead this past week, Ryan Strang, was a Phi Delta Theta fraternity brother. He was found at an off-campus home. Authorities found packages of kratom, a commercially available drug that has been derided as "gas station heroin," at both scenes. However, its role in either death was not immediately clear.

Phi Delta Theta has not been accused of any wrongdoing.

"The loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy," the fraternity said in a statement, in part. "Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them.

"These losses reinforce the importance of a collective commitment to health, safety, and well-being on college campuses today. We encourage the Phi Delta Theta community to keep the Strang family, the Mississippi Alpha Chapter, and everyone affected by these tragic losses in their thoughts."

Dangers like kratom did not exist when Lohse was in school, he said.

"There was no kratom, no tranq, no smoking bath salts, no fentanyl. Back then, the cocaine was more or less just cocaine. It wasn't like every time somebody did cocaine they could die."

OLE MISS TOXICOLOGY REPORTS EXPECTED SOON AND RESULTS MAY TRIGGER ANTI-FENTANYL LAW, OFFICIAL SAYS

At Penn State, prosecutors allege in court documents that pledges were allegedly coerced into cutting and packaging cocaine as part of an alleged organized drug ring led by former Sigma Chi member Agostino Abbatiello.

Lohse said, "When I was reading that the pledges were in the background doing that, I thought that was sort of amazing – but in a bad way, but also extremely brazen."

PENN STATE COCAINE BUST NETS 14 ARRESTS OVER ALLEGED PLEDGE COKE-CUTTING ‘INDOCTRINATION' RITUALS

Fraternity culture made more news this past week in Madison, Wisconsin, where police said they found roughly 30 partially clothed young men packed inside a sweltering basement, covered in food, condiments and other liquids – with several pledges showing signs of being physically assaulted.

The Madison Police Department said officers were dispatched to the Alpha Epsilon Pi (AEPi) house on Wednesday night and are investigating the hazing incident, with two people arrested.

"AEPi Headquarters takes the allegations involving our Pi Chapter in Madison, Wisconsin, extremely seriously," Jonathan Pierce, the fraternity's chief communications officer, said in a statement. "We will cooperate fully with the authorities investigating this matter."

"Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for. There is no place for it in AEPi," he added. "No exceptions. No excuses. We educate our members about their responsibility to ‘Be Your Brothers’ Keeper.’ This is not an optional value."

"It's a sad moment, for society, civilization," Lohse said about some of the recent headlines involving fraternity behavior. "These organizations should be forces of good. Young men need it more than ever. Young men are more adrift than ever, there's no moral leadership."

"There's a vacuum in the center of higher education and American society that used to be filled by God, by religion, by the church," he said, adding that it's "totally vacant now."

During his time as a brother at Sigma Alpha Epsilon, he said he was forced to "swim in a kiddie pool full of vomit while being urinated on," and "chug" vinegar or milk to the point that he and his fellow pledge brothers "would vomit" in a room covered with tarps.

FORMER MICHIGAN HOCKEY PLAYERS ALLEGE COACHES IGNORED YEARS OF ABUSIVE HAZING RITUALS

He also said he was forced into a small basement crawl space for a period of time. This was all in addition to constant coerced binge drinking, he said.

"We're talking like 10, 15 plus drinks," he said.

MIAMI SECRET SERVICE AGENT CHARGED IN NEAR-DEADLY FRATERNITY HAZING, OFFICIALS SAY

He said the unwritten "code of silence" or "omertà" contributes to these repeated hazing or drug-related issues within frats.

"The original 19th-century concept of the American fraternity is not what exists today," Lohse said.

THREE COLLEGE FRATS IN CROSSHAIRS AS HAZING CLAIMS OF BOOZE, BURNS AND HOSPITAL TRIPS SPARK CRACKDOWN: SCHOOL

"Essentially, you can look at a modern fraternity like a criminal organization. In most states, the unique behavioral attributes of a fraternity cross into criminal statutes—whether misdemeanor hazing or serious felony drug trafficking. You need a code of silence to protect that."

He went on to say, "the organization forces the individual to compromise their own identity for the collective, taking something from its members to ensure the system perpetuates itself over time."

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Following the hazing incidents during Lohse's time as a student, SAE was suspended from Dartmouth for the last 10 years and re-recognized in August, The Darmouth student-run paper reported.

When asked what advice he would offer students considering Greek life at major universities, Lohse stopped short of telling students flatly to avoid fraternities. Instead, Lohse urges young men to calculate the "opportunity cost" before pledging.

"Consider that the upside benefit, while maybe not zero, pales in comparison to the downside risk," Lohse said, advising incoming students to reflect on what they truly want out of higher education.

SEND US A TIP

GOT A TIP?

"Think about what you actually want out of college. Who do you really want to be around, and who is actually going to be there to help you? I think you'll find that a fraternity isn't going to provide that."

Judson Horras, president and CEO of the North American Interfraternity Conference, told Fox News Digital that "student safety is our members' highest priority. The NIC has adopted enhanced health and safety guidelines and co-led advocacy to pass tougher anti-hazing laws in more than a dozen states, as well as the federal Stop Campus Hazing Act."

Regarding the Ole Miss students' deaths, Horras said: "We are heartbroken by the loss of two University of Mississippi students, one of whom was a fraternity member. Our sympathies are with both families and the Ole Miss community. We will continue working with universities and families to keep every student safe."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Sigma Alpha Epsilon, Phi Delta Theta and Abbatiello's attorney for comment.

item.title: Mount Shasta climber recounts harrowing 500-foot slide, overnight crawl to safety: report
item.description: Zubayir Kazi lost all his supplies during a failed glissade down Mount Shasta's Avalanche Gulch and crawled through the night with grave injuries.
item.content:encoded:
A California climber who survived a roughly 500-foot slide down Mount Shasta is recounting how he crawled through the night after losing his supplies and suffering serious injuries.

Zubayir Kazi, 24, of San Jose, told NBC Bay Area that he reached the summit Sept. 10, during his first icy summit attempt before things went wrong on his descent.

"Everything I had with me just goes out of my hand and I find myself flying down the mountain," Kazi said.

NOVICE CLIMBER SURVIVES 1,500-FOOT DROP ON CALIFORNIA'S MOUNT SHASTA AFTER HELICOPTER RESCUE DELAYED BY CLOUDS

Kazi said he lost his food, water, cellphone and light, leaving him alone without a way to call for help.

"My mentality became very one dimensional. I don’t know what’s the optimal thing to do, but I just know that I have to go lower because if I stay here and fall asleep, I’m going to die," he said.

The U.S. Forest Service previously told Fox News Digital that Kazi lost control while attempting to glissade, or slide, down the snow and ice-covered Avalanche Gulch after reaching the summit. He suffered significant lacerations and injuries to his feet.

NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING'

Swelling forced Kazi to remove his boots, and he crawled through the night until reaching Horse Camp Cabin. His friends reported him missing after losing contact with him, prompting a multi-agency search.

A hiker found Kazi inside the cabin the following day and provided him with food and water before rescuers arrived.

"When the officers came in, it was the first time I really realized how badly I was injured. They said 'You have no skin behind your leg'," Kazi said.

HIKER, 61, BATTLES AGONIZING INJURY ON GRUELING CLIMB, RESETS DISLOCATED SHOULDER HIMSELF

Kazi told NBC Bay Area that he suffered significant skin and nerve damage and serious internal complications. He said doctors told him he could have died within hours.

The Forest Service previously praised Kazi for knowing his route and telling friends about his climbing plans, while urging climbers to carry backup electronics, allow enough daylight and prepare to self-rescue.

Kazi said the ordeal changed his approach to climbing.

"It is very important to fully and properly account for all of the requirements and safety considerations necessary to complete a hike like this and not miss a single one — and I'd say to definitely not go alone," Kazi said.

Fox News Digital could not locate contact information for Kazi to seek additional comment.

Fox News Digital's Bonny Chu contributed to this report.

Spencer wrote that he believed the diatribe was the result of Charles’ "pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death."

After the excerpt from the book was released last week, Buckingham Palace issued a rare statement.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," the statement said.

Spencer wrote that after falling in love with heart surgeon Dr. Hasnat Khan following her divorce, Diana had the "naïve yet impossible" dream of moving to South Africa — where Spencer lived at the time — with her boyfriend because England had become "intolerable" to her.

"Might they, she dared hope, move there together, and carve out a life?" he wrote.

He said she dreamed that Khan could work at a hospital in Cape Town, and they could live "happily — normally — nearby" her brother.

"The other side of the world seemed to offer the possibility of asylum," he wrote.

INSIDE PRINCESS DIANA AND JFK JR.'S SECRET MEETING THAT FUELED ROMANCE RUMORS FOR DECADES

Spencer said that Diana once asked him if he thought she’d make a good American first lady, explaining that one of her "many powerful aging American suitors, keen to secure her as the ultimate trophy wife, had told her he was sure to win the presidency if she married him."

He said that Diana was more "titillated" by the idea of living in the White House than by the prospect of marrying the "would-be elderly husband."

Diana, he said, had a "mischievous attraction to reinventing herself in a role that would make her enemies in the British Royal Family sick with jealousy, while ushering in an era of glamour in the White House that would surely have surpassed even that of the Jackie Kennedy years."

Despite "Panorama" reporter Martin Bashir allegedly telling Diana a series of falsehoods, including that she was being surveilled by MI6, that Prince William was unwittingly bugging her through a device on his watch and that her children’s nanny had aborted Prince Charles' child after an affair, Diana almost canceled the interview, Spencer said.

He wrote that the princess pulled out a few days before the interview was scheduled to take place.

But Bashir and the show’s executive producer persisted, Spencer wrote. He said they arranged a clandestine meeting in a parking garage, where Spencer believes they persuaded Diana that her life was in "imminent" danger and that doing the interview was the best way to protect herself.

Spencer said he had a conversation with Charles after his own father’s funeral, during which Charles told him he was "lucky" his father had died because he got to inherit when he was "so young."

Charles allegedly said that while Spencer was inheriting his ancestral home of Althorp in his 20s, the prince complained that he was 43 and employed 50 people, "but my parents insist on treating me like — like a child!"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

He also wrote that when a senior courtier told Queen Elizabeth that Charles resented a reprimand she had delivered through the courtier, the queen dismissed the concern, telling him: "He even resented it when I taught him the alphabet."

Spencer also wrote that Diana told him early in her relationship with the prince that the queen had once considered having Charles’ ears pinned back because their "protrusion" had caused him to be teased at school and mocked by the media. Prince Philip put a stop to it, however, according to Spencer. 

Spencer added that he didn’t know whether the story was true, but said Diana believed it.

Later in the book, Spencer wrote that when Diana first told him she planned to divorce Charles, she claimed that the prince was "in love with his valet."

Spencer said he found the claim improbable, but didn't press her for more information because he was focused on the realization that she was ending her marriage and her "dreams."

Spencer wrote that his sister had "traditionally feminine" interests, which included collecting numerous stuffed animals as a child. She loved flowers, especially forget-me-nots, listened to the Beatles and David Bowie, and liked the soap opera "Crossroads."

As she got older, Spencer wrote that she "devoured" romance novels by Barbara Cartland, whom he said mainly wrote about aristocratic men pursuing virginal women and eventually living happily ever after.

She also once told Spencer that she had watched the equally romantic "The Sound of Music" 16 times.

Spencer's book was released nearly a year before the 30th anniversary of Diana's death. Diana was killed in a car crash in Paris on Aug. 31, 1997.
